Emoji networks: edges worth drawing

Source: vignettes/emoji-networks.Rmd
emoji-networks.Rmd

Which emoji are used together is a network question, and emoji_pairs() returns exactly the edge list a network package wants. The trap is that the edge list it returns by default is mostly noise, and a layout draws noise as confidently as it draws structure. This article builds an emoji network that is worth drawing: weighted by an association measure, thresholded on frequency, and checked against what the emoji-network literature says such networks look like.

library(tidyEmoji)
library(dplyr)

posts <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "ata_tweets.csv",
                              package = "tidyEmoji"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")

Counts first, and why they are not enough

One row per pair of distinct emoji that appear in the same post, with the number of posts in which they do:

edges <- posts %>% emoji_pairs(full_text)
edges
#> # A tibble: 213 × 3
#>    item1 item2     n
#>    <chr> <chr> <int>
#>  1 😂    😭       10
#>  2 😂    😩        4
#>  3 😂    🙄        3
#>  4 😭    🙄        3
#>  5 💕    🥰        2
#>  6 💞    🥺        2
#>  7 💯    🤷🏽‍♂️        2
#>  8 😂    🤔        2
#>  9 😂    🤣        2
#> 10 😂    🤷🏼‍♀️        2
#> # ℹ 203 more rows

edges %>% count(n, name = "pairs")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>       n pairs
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1   200
#> 2     2     9
#> 3     3     2
#> 4     4     1
#> 5    10     1

200 of the 213 edges (93.9%) are a single post. A graph drawn from all of them is one post’s worth of evidence per line, and the few heavy edges belong to the emoji that are common everywhere, which pair with everything because they are common, not because they are related.

Weight by association, then threshold on frequency

Two changes fix this, and they do different jobs.

  • An association measure scores each pair against what its two emoji’s own frequencies predict, so a common emoji no longer wins every edge. measure = "dice" is 2 * n / (n1 + n2), with n1 and n2 the posts holding each emoji: 1 for a pair never seen apart, near 0 for a pair that is mostly apart. "ppmi" and "log_odds" are the alternatives; see ?emoji_pairs.
  • A frequency threshold removes the edges seen too rarely to mean anything. An association measure cannot do this on its own: a pair seen in one post, whose two emoji appear nowhere else, scores the maximum Dice of 1.
weighted <- posts %>%
  emoji_pairs(full_text, measure = "dice") %>%
  filter(n >= 2)

weighted
#> # A tibble: 13 × 4
#>    item1 item2     n   dice
#>    <chr> <chr> <int>  <dbl>
#>  1 💞    🥺        2 0.222 
#>  2 💕    🥰        2 0.182 
#>  3 💯    🤷🏽‍♂️        2 0.182 
#>  4 😂    😭       10 0.121 
#>  5 😭    🙄        3 0.0659
#>  6 😂    😩        4 0.064 
#>  7 😂    🙄        3 0.0526
#>  8 😭    🥰        2 0.0460
#>  9 😭    🥴        2 0.0440
#> 10 😂    🤷🏼‍♀️        2 0.0417
#> 11 😂    🤔        2 0.0396
#> 12 😂    🥰        2 0.0364
#> 13 😂    🤣        2 0.0339

That is the honest network for this corpus: 13 edges. Two thousand posts holding 900 emoji are too few for a network of more than a handful of emoji, and it is better to know that than to draw the 213-edge version. A corpus of hundreds of thousands of posts, or one pooled by user or by conversation with doc_id, gives a graph with real structure.

Into a network package

The edge list feeds igraph (or tidygraph) directly, with the association measure as the edge weight:

g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  weighted[, c("item1", "item2", "dice", "n")], directed = FALSE)

igraph::vcount(g)
#> [1] 14
igraph::ecount(g)
#> [1] 13
igraph::components(g)$no
#> [1] 3

Community detection then groups emoji that are used together more than chance; Louvain with the Dice weight is a reasonable default:

set.seed(2026)   # Louvain breaks ties at random; fix them for a stable answer
communities <- igraph::cluster_louvain(g, weights = igraph::E(g)$dice)
split(igraph::V(g)$name, igraph::membership(communities))
#> $`1`
#> [1] "💞" "🥺"
#> 
#> $`2`
#> [1] "💕" "🥰"
#> 
#> $`3`
#> [1] "💯"    "🤷🏽‍♂️"
#> 
#> $`4`
#> [1] "😂"    "😭"    "🙄"    "😩"    "🥴"    "🤷🏼‍♀️" "🤔"    "🤣"

Drawing it is a job for a graph-plotting package. With ggraph installed, and ragg as the graphics device so the glyphs render in colour:

library(ggraph)
ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = dice), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 6) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2)) +
  theme_void()

Sanity checks for a bigger corpus

Studies of emoji co-occurrence networks on large Twitter samples (Fede et al., 2018; Alsaif et al., 2021) report two properties, and both make good checks that a network is measuring structure rather than sampling noise:

  • the degree distribution is heavy-tailed: a few emoji connect to very many, most connect to a few;
  • most emoji fall into a handful of communities.

Both are one line once the graph exists. On a network of a dozen nodes they say little; on a real one, a degree table with no tail or a community count close to the node count is a sign that the threshold was set too low:

table(igraph::degree(g))
#> 
#>  1  2  3  4  7 
#> 10  1  1  1  1
length(communities)
#> [1] 4

Directed sequences

emoji_pairs(directed = TRUE) orders each pair by first appearance in the post, so the edge from one emoji to another counts the posts where the first came first. The same measures apply to that ordered event, and emoji_ngrams() gives the strictly consecutive version for Markov-style models of emoji sequences.

References

Alsaif H, Roesch P, Othman S (2021). Analyzing Co-occurrence Networks of Emojis on Twitter. In Intelligent Computing, Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-80126-7_7

Fede H, Herrera I, Mahdi Seyednezhad SM, Menezes R (2018). Representing Emoji Usage Using Directed Networks: A Twitter Case Study. In Complex Networks & Their Applications VI. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-72150-7_67
